'''''Protea laurifolia''''', also known as the '''grey-leaf sugarbush''',<ref name=SANBI/><ref name=BioEx>{{cite web |title=''Protea laurifolia'' (Grey-leaf sugarbush) |url=http://biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/proteaceae/protea_laurifolia.htm |website=Biodiversity Explorer |publisher=Iziko - Museums of South Africa |access-date=26 July 2020}}</ref><ref name=ProAtlWeb>{{Cite web |url=https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/sugar2.htm |title=Bearded Sugarbushes - ''Proteas'' |date=11 March 1998 |website=Protea Atlas Project Website |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref> is a [[shrub]] from [[South Africa]].<ref name=ProAtlWeb/><ref name=smgrow>{{cite web |url=https://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2352 |title=''Protea laurifolia'' 'Rose Mink' |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=www.smgrowers.com |publisher=San Marcos Growers |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref> It is native to the [[Cape Provinces]] of South Africa.<ref>{{GRIN | access-date=11 August 2015}}</ref>

Another [[vernacular name]] for this species is '''laurel sugarbush'''. In [[Afrikaans language|Afrikaans]] this species is known by the common names of {{lang|af|louriersuikerbos}}, {{lang|af|lourier-suikerbos}}, {{lang|af|suikerbos}} and {{lang|af|suikerkan}}.<ref name=SANBI/>

''Protea laurifolia'' was first [[scientific description|described]] by [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] in 1806.<ref name=IPNI/>

==Description==
''Protea laurifolia'' is a tall, erect shrub which can grow up to eight metres in height.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> The [[leaf|leaves]] are grey to bluish green and short-stalked with horny margins.<ref name=vanWyk1997>{{cite book |last=van Wyk |first=Braam |last2=van Wyk |first2=Piet |date=1997 |title=Field Guide to trees of South Africa |location=Cape Town |publisher=Struik |pages=216, 217 |isbn=1-86825-922-6}}</ref> It flowers from mid-Autumn to early Winter, or from April to November.<ref name=BioEx/><ref name=ProAtlWeb/> The plant is [[monoecious]] with both sexes in each flower.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

It is similar to [[Protea neriifolia|''P. neriifolia'']], but has a more westerly distribution. ''P. neriifolia'' has sessile (no [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]) leaves, which curve upwards and are often somewhat more greenish.<ref name=vanWyk1997/>

==Distribution==
This plant species is [[endemic]] to South Africa, but occurs in both the [[Northern Cape|Northern]] and [[Western Cape]] provinces.<ref name=SANBI/> It is found from [[Nieuwoudtville]] to [[Franschhoek]] and [[Anysberg]].<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> In the Western Cape it occurs in the Elands Kloof in the [[Hottentots Holland Mountains]] and the [[Witzenberg Local Municipality|Agterwitzenberg Vlakte]] in the [[Skurweberg Pass|Skurweberg Mountains]], part of the [[Koue Bokkeveld Mountains|Koue Bokkeveld]] mountain range.<ref name=BioEx/>

==Ecology==
It grows in sandy or [[granite]] soils, at altitudes of {{Convert|400 to 1,200|m}}.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> It is usually found in a [[fynbos]] [[habitat]], but sometimes also grows on [[shale]], or in [[renosterveld]] or scrubland.<ref name=SANBI/>

The adult plants are killed by the periodic [[wildfire]]s of its habitat, but its seeds survive these events. The fruits are woody and persistent, which means they are retained on the plant after [[Plant senescence|senescence]].<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> The burnt skeletons of trees release the seeds from the retained dry [[Pseudanthium|flower heads]] in the season following a wildfire.<ref name=BioEx/> The seeds are dispersed by means of the wind.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/>

==Horticulture==
The hybrid [[cultivar]] 'Rose Mink' was selected by Dennis Perry and is sold in the US as an [[ornamental plant]]. It is fairly [[Hardiness (plants)|frost-hardy]] in southern Californian gardens.<ref name=smgrow>{{cite web |url=https://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2352 |title=''Protea laurifolia'' 'Rose Mink' |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=www.smgrowers.com |publisher=San Marcos Growers |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref>

==Conservation==
The status of world population is not considered threatened.<ref name=ProAtlWeb/> It was first assessed as '[[least concern]]' by the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] (SANBI) in 2009. According to the 2019 SANBI assessment the overall population is decreasing, but it was nonetheless still assessed as 'least concern'.<ref name=SANBI/>
